sec.title: Background
sec.p: Older adults are particularly vulnerable to social isolation and loneliness, and these factors amplify modifiable cardiovascular (CVD) risk factors for those with existing CVD. A range of interventions have been reported in the literature. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the impact of non-pharmacological interventions targeting loneliness and social isolation experienced by older adults in this target group, who are living independently or in residential facilities.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Four databases (Embase, Medline, CINAHL, and PsycINFO) were searched. Papers were screened by two independent reviewers and included if they were in English, evaluated interventions addressing loneliness, social isolation, or social support in older adults (mean age ≥ 55) with CVD. Eligible papers included qualitative and quantitative designs with outcomes related to quality of life, lifestyle factors, or cardiovascular biomarkers. Randomised controlled trials were assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (Version 2). Methodological quality was evaluated using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) or the Mixed Methods Assessment Tool (MMAT). The replicability and reporting of papers was documented against the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) checklist and the RE-AIM framework.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 8451 papers were identified, hand-searching identified a further 16. 5396 papers were screened for title and abstract after de-duplication. One hundred and eighteen papers were assessed for inclusion. Twelve papers were included, representing 11 studies, with interventions delivered to 651 participants across seven countries. Group-based activities, particularly those combining exercise and education, were the most common and consistently demonstrated improvements in social support, psychological wellbeing, and quality of life. Four papers reported statistically significant improvements in social support, while one reported a decline. Psychological outcomes improved in four papers, and quality of life improved in four out of five papers. Face-to-face group interventions demonstrated improvements across several key outcomes, including reduced loneliness, psychological wellbeing and quality of life.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This review suggests face-to-face group-based exercise and education programs may provide a basis for improving loneliness and social isolation in older adults with existing CVD. Further research is warranted given the limited number of studies that have targeted this population group and there is a need for high quality studies detailing reproducible interventions to guide evidence-based practice.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of mortality worldwide and a major contributor to disability [1]. Since 1990, the number of yearly deaths attributed to CVD has increased more than 48% and global prevalence has nearly doubled to approximately 523 million [2, 3]. It is predicted that by 2029, total healthcare costs of CVD in Australia will exceed $61 billion (AUD) [4]. Cardiovascular diseases encompass a range of conditions, of which ischemic heart disease and stroke are the most common [5]. Additional forms of CVD include peripheral arterial disease, rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart disease, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism [6]. For the purposes of this current systematic review, CVD will encompass all these conditions. The significant public health and economic burden of CVD may be attributed to an inability to adequately support at-risk populations and control risk factors leading to or amplifying this disease [7].

Older adults are at a higher risk of developing CVD than younger individuals [8]. Globally, the number of people aged 60 years and older is projected to increase from 1.1 billion in 2023 to over 1.4 billion by 2030 [9]. Age as a factor in CVD development may be related to the opportunity for exposure to the modifiable factors that affect some individuals more than others [10], with increased CVD risk for individuals from the age of 55 years [4]. Given the established burden of CVD in this age group, effective and innovative approaches to secondary prevention and management are of particular importance in those with existing CVD.

For older adults the issues of social isolation and loneliness are pertinent, and amplify the modifiable CVD risk factors [11]. Older adults are particularly vulnerable to social isolation and loneliness due to transitions that occur later in life, including decline in mobility and cognition, changes in living situations and loss of quality and quantity of social connections [12]. Additionally, social isolation and loneliness in the older adult population has been amplified by the Covid-19 pandemic and its requirement for social distancing and quarantine measures, further highlighting the need for effective strategies to reduce social isolation and loneliness in this population group [13]. Loneliness is an experience where a person perceives both the quantity and quality of their social interactions to be insufficient and has been described as a disconnect between desired and true social connections [8, 14]. Social isolation is defined as having few social relationships or roles or infrequent social contact [15]. Social isolation and loneliness are two interconnected but distinct concepts, whereby a person may be socially isolated, but not lonely or vice versa [15]. Social support is often defined as the perceived or actual availability of social contact, and those considered to be socially isolated or lonely tend to have lower levels of social support [16, 17]. Improving social support has been shown to reduce levels of social isolation and loneliness [18].

Compelling evidence links social isolation and loneliness to poorer cardiovascular and mental health outcomes [19] as well as an increased risk of early mortality [20] For patients with existing CVD, there are a variety of interventions available to manage disease burden and reduce risk of further disease. Interventions aimed at enhancing psychosocial wellbeing in patients with existing CVD [21–24] included pharmacological (e.g. anti-depressants) and non-pharmacological strategies such as environmental enrichment [21], peer-support [22, 23] and/or caregiver-oriented support [24]. A previous scoping review describes cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness, peer support, and multi-faceted cardiac rehabilitation programmes as strategies of enhancing social support for people living with CVD [24].

Previous research has identified a range of interventions aimed at enhancing social support among individuals with existing CVD [24]. However, further evaluation of interventions designed to facilitate social support and reduce loneliness in older adults with CVD is required. Additionally, using a systematic rather than scoping approach provides an opportunity to identify and retrieve international evidence, evaluate the quality of such evidence, and provide an assessment of their impact [25]. Therefore, this systematic review aims to evaluate non-pharmacological interventions targeting loneliness and social isolation experienced by older adults, with established CVD who are living independently or in residential facilities. This review sought to address the following research questions:

list-item.p: What is the impact of non-pharmacological interventions targeting loneliness and social isolation in older adults with CVD?
What is the impact of non-pharmacological interventions on physical and emotional wellbeing in older adults with CVD?

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This systematic review was conducted using methods described by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review (PRISMA) 2020 [26] guidelines and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023410953).

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: To be included, studies must have investigated non-pharmacological interventions aimed at loneliness and social isolation, which may include enhancing social support in older adults with CVD, who reside in the community or in residential facilities. Interventions needed to address the issue of loneliness or social isolation as previously defined, however they did not necessarily have to measure social support as an outcome. While definitions of older adults vary in the literature, for the purpose of this review, ‘older adults’ refers to the adults aged greater than 55 years. To adhere to this criterion, included studies were required to have a sample population with a mean age greater than 55 years or where the first standard deviation included participants aged greater than or equal to 50 years.

The search was limited to publications from 1 January 2000 onwards, due to the relevance of these papers to the current period and the increase in prominence of social support and related interventions. Studies must have reported outcomes that addressed physical and/or emotional wellbeing, and were evaluated using measures such as: physical examinations (e.g. palpation, percussion, auscultation), imaging (e.g. Electrocardiogram (ECG), chest x-rays), CVD measures (e.g. cholesterol, lipids, blood pressure etc.), and questionnaires or scales (e.g. Lubben Social Network Scale-6 [27]). Variations in outcome measures used were expected, but were acceptable, if they were related to social support, quality of life (QOL), psychological status or CVD assessment.

sec.title: Exclusion criteria
sec.p: Publications before the year 2000 and those not published in the English language were excluded as well as non-peer reviewed sources. This review included only studies published in English due to resource constraints, including the lack of access to translation services and non-English speaking reviewers. Editorials, conference abstracts, and studies that provided limited details or a perspective instead of evidence of outcomes such as narrative reviews were excluded. Additionally, papers where outcomes regarding the target population group of older adults could not be differentiated from younger population groups were also excluded. No other exclusion criteria were applied. All criteria are detailed in Table 1.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: Four electronic databases (Embase, Medline, CINAHL, and PSYCinfo) were searched for appropriate literature published from 1 January 2000 until June 2025. An academic librarian at the University of Newcastle was consulted to assist in our literature search. A Population, Intervention, Outcome (PIO) framework was adopted to create the selection of keywords in the search strategy and to formulate the review question. Population concepts related to older adults and cardiovascular disease, while intervention concepts included non-pharmacological interventions for social isolation and loneliness. The final database search strategy is outlined in Supplementary file 1. Reference lists of excluded systematic reviews were hand searched and checked for any relevant papers that may have been missed by the databases searched, with then being each considered at the title and abstract screening stage.

sec.title: Selection process
sec.p: Duplicates were removed. Pairs of researchers (KC, A.Blassey, CL, IP, JVW, SH, A.Brown and LB) independently screened all titles and abstracts in Covidence, an online tool for systematic review screening and data extraction [28]. Full text screening was conducted by pairs of reviewers (KC, A.Blassey, CL, IP, JVW, SH, A.Brown and LB). All conflicts over the eligibility of papers were resolved by a third team member or group consensus at each stage. To ensure inter-rater reliability, screening was initially conducted as a group and benchmarking occurred to ensure there was consistency in what was being included and excluded.

sec.title: Data collection process
sec.p: Pairs of researchers independently extracted relevant data (KC, A.Blassey, CL, A.Brown and JVW) from included papers and collated this data into a purpose-developed data extraction table using an Excel spreadsheet. The data extraction table included author and title information, intervention description, measures, outcomes (separated into domains of CVD, quality of life, psychological, and social isolation), findings, and conclusions. A second researcher (KC, A.Blassey, IP, SH, A.Brown, CL or JVW) reviewed data extraction for each paper to ensure there was consistency in what was being extracted.

sec.title: Bias and quality assessment
sec.p: Included RCTs were assessed by pairs of researchers using Version 2 of the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (ROB2) [29] to appraise the risk of bias in randomised studies. The ROB2 tool is structured into different domains of bias with focus on several aspects of the study, such as design, conduct and reporting. The stratification of papers into ‘low risk’, ‘some concerns’ and ‘high risk’ of bias was completed in accordance with the supplied algorithm.

The methodological quality of reporting in each of the papers was evaluated using the relevant (qualitative or randomised controlled trial) Critical Appraisal Skills Programme [30] (CASP) checklists. CASP checklists involve a series of questions examining the method by which trials are created, analysed and interpreted. Each question on the CASP tool is answered with “Yes”, “No” or “Can’t tell” by the appraiser [30]. When a CASP tool could not be used, due to the study not being compatible with the tool, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) tool was used [31]. Any discrepancies that arose between assessments were reviewed by a third team member (KS, A.Blassey, SH, CL, IP, A.Brown or JVW). Potential confounders (such as factors that increased exposure risk to CVD such as socioeconomic status, gender, and family history) were considered in the quality assessments.

Additionally, the replicability and reporting of papers was documented against the Template of Intervention Description and Replications (TIDieR) [32] checklist and the ‘Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance’ (RE-AIM) [33] tool to establish the replicability of their interventions. TIDier evaluates the completeness of reporting of an intervention through a 12-item checklist; this includes a description of the intervention, the rationale, the completeness of the methods (materials, procedures, etc.), tailoring and modifications of the study, and the planned and actual performance of the study (especially regarding fidelity) [32]. RE-AIM involves five domains each with a series of checklist items to evaluate the degree to which they are addressed. This tool aims to inspect the validity and sustainability of interventions and assess their feasibility in ‘real-world’ settings [33].
Quality and Risk of bias appraisals of studies was completed independently by one researcher, with the appraisals checked by a second researcher and any inconsistencies were discussed and resolved.

sec.title: Qualitative data Meta-Synthesis
sec.p: For studies using mixed methods and/or qualitative data, the qualitative themes and sub-themes were extracted from the included papers. This data was then summarised and developed into overarching themes through a meta-synthesis [34].

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p:
The PRISMA flow chart (see Fig. 1) reports the number of papers screened at each stage, including the number and reason for the exclusion of papers. A total of 8451 articles were identified across the four databases, with 3071 duplicates removed. After citation checking of excluded reviews, a further 16 articles were identified, resulting in 5396 articles for title and abstract screening. One hundred and eighteen articles were retrieved and assessed for inclusion, with 12 articles meeting the inclusion criteria [32, 35–43].Fig. 1

sec.title: Study and participant characteristics
sec.p: The 12 papers, representing 11 studies, included in this systematic review were conducted across seven countries (prominently in the USA, n = 4, see Table 2) and involved a total of 651 participants (range: 30–120) [32, 35–45]. One study was reported across two papers due to different outcome measures [37, 42], and will be referred to as one study or two papers throughout. The age of participants ranged from 63.6 to 73.5 years. The types of CVD experienced by participants included stroke [36, 40, 44, 45] coronary heart disease [37, 39, 46] and heart failure [38, 41–43, 47]. Study designs varied across the studies and included randomised controlled trials (n = 9) [35, 36, 39–41, 43–46], a comparative (before and after) study (n = 1, across two papers) [37, 42] and a quasi-experimental study (n = 1) [38]. sec.title: Description of interventions
sec.p: Group activities were the main delivery method for interventions in eight studies [36, 38–41, 43–45, 47]. Of these, three studies involved exercise and education, including group classes [37, 38, 42, 46], three involved education only [39, 40, 44], and one involved exercise only [43]. Three studies utilised a peer mentorship program that included weekly contact with participants [35, 41, 45]. Only one study incorporated tailored discharge with daily group messaging services [36]. A diverse range of outcome measures were recorded, nine studies reported on social isolation and loneliness [35–38, 40–42, 45, 46], five studies reported on CVD measures [37, 38, 40–42, 44], seven studies assessed psychological outcomes [35, 37–40, 42, 45, 46], seven studies measured QOL [36–38, 40, 45, 46] and two studies reported additional qualitative data [37, 42, 43].

sec.title: Social support outcomes
sec.p:
Of the nine studies that measured social support outcomes [35–38, 40–42, 45, 46], three reported statistically significant improvements from baseline [36, 37, 42, 45] and one reported a statistically significant decline [41] (see Tables 3 and 4). Four different tools were used to measure social support, including the Social Support Score (SSRS), the Medical Outcomes Study Social Support Survey Questionnaire (MOS-SSS), the UCLA Social Support Inventory (UCLA-SSI) and the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS). Using the Social Support Survey Questionnaire (MOS-SSS), Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) [37, 42] observed a statistically significant change. Tangible and affectionate social outcomes improved, in addition to positive social interaction and emotional/informational outcomes. Hu et al. (2022) used the Social Support Score (SSRS) and reported improvements in the intervention group score from baseline. In a study by Riegel et al. (2004) a statistically significant decrease in the intervention group’s support reciprocity at 90 days, as determined by the UCLA Social Support Inventory (UCLA-SSI) [41]. Other social measures, including ‘support desired and sought’ and ‘satisfaction with support received’, had no statistically significant differences between groups. Wan et al. (2024) reported a statistically significant increase in social support, as determined by the MSPSS, in addition to an improvement in social participation at both follow up time points. sec.title: Cardiovascular disease outcomes
sec.p: Five studies reported on CVD outcomes [37, 38, 40–42, 44], of which, three reported changes from baseline [40] (see Tables 3 and 4). Cardiovascular disease outcomes included dyspnoea, fatigue, 6-minute walking tests (6MWT), cholesterol panels, time to readmission for cardiovascular causes/death from cardiovascular causes and systolic blood pressure. One study reported on dyspnoea, fatigue, and 6MWT [37, 42], another study reported on cholesterol panels [38], two studies reported on time to re-hospitalisation [40, 41] and one study reported on systolic blood pressure [44]. Hui (2006 and 2009) reported significant improvements in dyspnoea, fatigue and 6MWT. Kreikebaum et al. (2011) evaluated CVD outcomes using cholesterol panels taken throughout the duration of the intervention [38]. Results reported a significant decrease in cholesterol and triglycerides levels with a significant increase in HDL levels. Riegel et al. (2004) demonstrated decreased time to re-hospitalisation and increased readmission rates when compared to the control group, which was considered a deterioration. Dhand et al. (2025) found no statistically significant difference in systolic blood pressure at follow up.

sec.title: Psychological outcomes
sec.p: Psychological outcome measures were reported in seven studies (see Tables 3 and 4) [35, 37–40, 42, 45, 46]. A variety of scales were used to assess change in psychological status, including the; Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), Beck Depression Inventory Second Edition (BDI-II), Shortened Perceived Stress Scale (SPSS), Centre for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), and Positive Affect Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS). These scales aimed to measure depression (n = 3) [35, 38, 39], anxiety and depression (n = 3) [37, 45, 46] and positive and negative affect (n = 1) [40]. Four of the studies reported a statistically significant improvement in psychological outcome measures from baseline (see Table 4) [37–39, 42, 45]. These included Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) and Wan et al. (2024), using the HADS, Kriekebaum et al. (2011) [38], using the BDI-II and SPSS, and Lin et al. (2019) [39], using the CES-D. Three studies found no statistically significant differences in psychological outcomes [35, 40, 46].

sec.title: Quality of Life (QOL) outcomes
sec.p: QOL outcome measures were reported in five studies, (see Tables 3 and 4) [36–38, 40, 45, 46]. Scales used for QOL were validated and included the World Health Organisation Quality of LifeScale (WHOQoL-Bref), the Short-Form 36 Health Survey Version 2.0 (SF-36v2), the RAND 36 and the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D-5 L). Four studies reported significant improvements in QOL post intervention [37, 38, 45, 46]. Two studies used the WHOQoL-Bref, Harrington et al. (2010) and Hu et al. (2022), both reported improvements from baseline. Kreikebaum et al. (2011) reported significant changes using the SF-36v2 and the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) from baseline to completion. Wan et al. (2024) reported improvements in QOL for the intervention group compared to control group immediately post intervention, but not at 3 month follow up. The remaining study, using the RAND 36, found no significant differences [40].

sec.title: Qualitative themes
sec.p:
Two studies, Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) and Yeh et al. (2016), reported on patient experiences of the intervention using qualitative methods (see Table 5). Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) conducted a focus group in the final week of their intervention and reported three thematic topics with several sub-themes. Yeh et al. (2016) conducted semi-structured interviews for their control (standard care) and intervention (additional group Tai Chi sessions) groups and reported several themes specific to the intervention group and across both the control and intervention groups [43]. A meta-synthesis [34] of the data was developed into four meta-themes: ‘open to connect and interact with others,’ ‘transformational education for improved health,’ ‘empowered to improve one’s own physical health,’ and ‘unforeseen benefits’ see Table 5 (Qualitative themes from included studies). The meta-theme ‘open to connect and interact with others’, reported on the improvements in social support and contact that were mostly attributed to participants being part of a group with people of similar health status to themselves. Improved mindfulness, empathy, motivation, and other major social components were likewise attributed to these aspects of the interventions. Regarding ‘transformational education for improved health’, the benefits of health education was identified as a major reason for participation in the intervention. Gaining an improved understanding of their disease and the benefits of the educational component were described through a sense of control, efficacy, and empowerment. The theme ‘empowered to improve one’s own physical health’ related to the benefits of the exercise-based interventions and linked the sub-themes relating to improved physical function and health, and confidence regarding their participation in exercise or physical activity. sec.title: Quality assessments: CASP and MMAT
sec.p:
Quality assessments are summarised in Table 6 (Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) and Cochrane Risk of Bias Version 2 (ROB2)) with the results of the CASP tool. Yeh (2016) [43] was the only qualitative study assessed with the CASP tool. The paper was assessed to be of very high quality. The only question reported as “Can’t tell” was number 7 which related to the comprehensive report of intervention effects, all other questions were assessed as “Yes”. Of the quantitative studies, the scores of all papers included were very similar in quality. All papers clearly addressed the research question and randomised assignments of participants in interventions. All participants were accounted for at the conclusion of the intervention and the effects of the interventions were reported comprehensively. Riegel (2004) was of the lowest quality according to the checklist due to the non-blinding of participants and investigators, baseline differences between groups, as well as researcher uncertainty regarding blinding of participants analysing the outcomes, whether experimental benefits outweighed the harms/cost, and whether the experimental intervention provided greater value to people in the researchers care than any other interventions [41].Table 6

The MMAT results are summarised in Table 6 (Mixed Methods Assessment Tool (MMAT) results for non-randomised quantitative studies) [31]; three papers required this assessment, as they were not compatible with CASP tool [30]. Kreikebaum et al. (2011) scored lowest with this tool; due to a lack of information on the demographics and comparison group, and due to the comparison group not being collected for research purposes. Hui et al. (2006) and Woo et al. (2009) scored lower, regarding discrepancies between the 2006 [37] and 2009 [42] publications of the same study; the latter publication had additional data from another study published alongside it with redactions made to its method that were not present in the original paper.Table 7

sec.title: Risk of bias
sec.p: The RoB 2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias of RCTs and is summarised in Table 7 [26]. Yeh et al. (2016) had a high risk score due to lack of blinding of participants and intervention providers, as well as inconsistent non-protocol interventions provided between intervention and control groups (control group received two education sessions per week and a weekly education pamphlet whereas the intervention group received only a weekly education pamphlet) [43]. Colella et al. (2018) acquired some concerns of bias due to a lack of information on data analysis in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan finalised before unblinded outcome data was available [35]. Assessment of Harrington et al. (2010) [46] indicated some concerns of bias with respect to its lack of blinding and the possibility that its lower completion rate (68–75%) may have also contributed to its bias in terms of reporting of results. Similarly, Hu et al. (2022) was assessed, indicating some concerns of bias due to a lack of blinding of participants and researchers [36]. Lin et al. (2019) was the only paper that returned with low risk of bias [39]. Nahlen Bose et al. (2016) was assessed to have a high risk of bias due to a lack of blinding of participants and intervention providers, and some non-adherence to the intervention which may have affected outcomes [40]. Riegel et al. (2004) was also assessed to have a high-risk score for concerns in multiple domains [41]. Firstly, there were baseline differences in the intervention groups that suggested a problem with the randomisation process itself. Secondly, there was no explicit confirmation of blinding of participants in the trial. Thirdly, there was non-adherence to the assigned intervention that potentially affected participants’ outcomes. Lastly, there were inconsistencies in the data available for all randomised participants; 88 were randomised, 58 had data for self-care and 57 had data for social support. This missing data has a possibility of confounding the true value of the other data presented.

sec.title: Reporting and reproducibility of interventions
sec.p:
The TIDieR [32] and RE-AIM [33] checklists were used to document the quality of description, and in turn the replicability, of interventions. The results of the TIDieR assessment are available in Table 7. Of the 12 items comprising the TIDieR checklist, all papers addressed or partially addressed at least seven items (range = 7–12) [32]. Riegel et al. (2004) described their intervention with the most completeness. Papers by Lin et al. (2019) and Hui et al. (2006) provided the least amount of detail, with Hui et al. (2006) and Woo et al. (2009) describing the same parent study. However, Woo et al. (2009) provided more detail on the intervention and thus scored better with the TIDieR checklist [32]. When the RE-AIM criteria [33] were applied, Riegel et al. (2004) and Harrington et al. (2010) scored well and Kreikebaum et al. (2011) performed poorly. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review of non pharmacological interventions targeting loneliness, social isolation and/or social support for older adults with CVD indicates that most types of interventions improved psychosocial wellbeing outcomes. However, changes in CVD outcomes could not be attributed to interventions that were focused on enhanced social support as these also included other lifestyle components (such as exercise). Programs focusing on group activities, incorporating exercise and education, were superior to or as effective as routine care in improving social support, QOL and psychological outcomes [36–41, 43, 47]. Group messaging [36] was also found to be effective at improving social support and QOL, and peer-mentor programs [35, 41] produced similar outcomes to usual care across all domains. This review noted the impact of face-to-face group-based interventions on improving loneliness and social isolation in older patients with CVD. Studies with face-to-face interventions [37–40, 42, 43, 46] had statistically significant improvements in most outcomes assessed. Studies that used non-face-to-face interventions, including phone calls and online WeChat accounts, reported varied levels of effectiveness [35, 36, 41]. Hu et al. (2022) utilised a tailored discharge plan and online WeChat account to facilitate information and programs to patients [36]. Similar to the results reported in the Clayton 2019 review noting a positive change with use of a peer support app, Hu et al. (2022) reported significant improvements in both social and QOL outcomes [24]. Whilst the impact of the WeChat account on psychological and CVD outcomes was not assessed, this suggests that the use of online interventions to address social support issues in the future would be worthwhile. Multiple prior studies found no consequential improvement in social support with the use of a phone call-based intervention [24, 47, 48]. Comparably, Colella et al. (2018) and Riegel et al. (2004) both had phone calls as a component of their program however observed no positive change. The lack of improvement in these studies may be attributed to the overall type of intervention being peer support-based and may not solely be placed on the telephone communication aspect. While face-to-face group-based interventions show promise clinically, the critical appraisal of these papers indicated some areas of concern (particularly related to the blinding of participants and researchers). Future research into such interventions using robust methods is warranted.

Studies with group-based education and exercise programs demonstrated impact on both social and CVD outcomes as well as QOL and psychological outcomes [37, 38, 42, 46]. Notably, this contrasts the outcomes of the review by Clayton (2019) who reported that cardiac rehabilitation programs (CRP), containing similar elements, had no positive effect on social support. This difference in findings may be due to the CRPs focusing on individual development supported by a facilitator in a group, whereas studies in this current systematic review utilised the group environment as a component of their intervention. A decline in adherence to health behaviours following the conclusion of CRPs was noted by Clayton’s (2019) review. This raises concerns regarding the long-term effectiveness of interventions described in this current systematic review, as effectiveness post-intervention was not assessed in many of the studies. Further research regarding the long-term impact is needed.

The two studies that demonstrated improvements in CVD outcomes, Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) and Kreikebaum et al. (2011), both utilised interventions that incorporated exercise, education, and encouraged a better dietary intake. Interventions involving exercise, education and dietary change have established evidence that demonstrates their effectiveness in the secondary prevention of CVD and they have been incorporated into standard cardiac rehabilitation practice [49]. Hence it would not be appropriate to attribute the improvement in CVD to solely the social aspects of these interventions. This is further supported by a lack of statistically significant changes reported by the remaining studies that did not include an exercise-based intervention. The role of social aspects of these interventions cannot be clearly attributed to the resulting outcomes as papers did not report accounting for other confounders in their design or analysis. Hui et al. (2006 & 2009) and Yeh et al. (2016) both included qualitative aspects to their study; their key themes reported that the social aspect of these studies encouraged patient participation in the primarily exercise-based interventions.

In line with findings reported by the Clayton review (2019), none of the peer support interventions included in this review demonstrated a statistically significant increase in social support. Given this, peer mentor programs alone are unlikely to be beneficial in increasing social support in patients with CVD. It should be noted, however, Riegel et al. (2004) demonstrated statistically significant increases in readmission for heart failure and health care utilisation which the authors attributed to increased patient understanding of their disease. As the study did not measure patient understanding of their disease in its measures, further research with appropriate measures would be required to give further insights.

This review had several strengths in its methodology and approach. The review had a well-defined and specific research question that focused on assessing the impact of interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness in older adults with CVD. The search strategy used in this review was thorough, as it involved searching across four different databases. To minimise errors in the search terms and enhance accuracy, the researchers sought assistance from an experienced librarian with expertise in academic searching. This collaboration helped refine the search process and reduce the risk of missing relevant studies. The researchers employed recognized checklists such as CASP, MMAT, and ROB2 to assess the quality of the included papers, and TiDier and RE-AIM to assess reporting and reproducibility of interventions [29–32]. These checklists provided structured frameworks for evaluating various aspects of the research, including methodological transparency, study quality, and potential biases. Lastly, the involvement of multiple reviewers in screening, conflict resolution, data extraction, and quality assessment ensured reliability and consistency throughout the study.

Several limitations should be acknowledged in this review. There were challenges related to the lack of standardized measures for social support and difficulties in accurately measuring social support, as evidenced by Riegel’s work [41]. As a result, there was insufficient data to answer the research questions related to effectiveness categorically by means of a meta-analysis. Another limitation stems from the lack of complete data in some studies, as not all outcomes were assessed uniformly across all included studies. Similarly, the heterogeneity of the CVD conditions reported in each study and the severity of these limits the ability to make categorical recommendations. The application of the ROB2 tool revealed that a considerable proportion of included studies exhibited a moderate to high risk of bias, which could potentially compromise the overall validity and reliability of the study’s findings [29]. However, this bias risk could be mostly attributed to an inability to blind, due to the nature of the interventions in these studies.

To examine the potential impact of this review’s findings on future practice, it is important to first explore the nature of current guidelines and compare them to the studies included in this systematic review. As reported by the Australian Cardiovascular Health and Rehabilitation Association [49] and the Australian Heart Foundation [50], there are certain components and domains that need to be addressed in cardiac rehabilitation. These are classically defined as; referral and access to services, assessment and short-term monitoring, recovery and long-term maintenance, lifestyle and behaviour modification, medication adherence, developing heart health knowledge, and psychosocial wellbeing. While all domains typically have strict guidelines outlining how cardiovascular outcomes can be improved, often psychosocial wellbeing is approached in a vague manner. The Australian Heart Foundation states that while depression screening does not directly lead to improved outcomes in populations with CVD, it has been shown that patients with depression and CVD, have worse outcomes overall [51]. This further outlines the need for a more direct approach to interventions that target social isolation and psychosocial wellbeing of patients with CVD. The outcomes measured varied between studies ranging from minimally to substantially statistically significant. Hence, it would be useful to focus on the interventions provided by the five studies with positive outcomes in terms of applications to older CVD patients in the community. These interventions included group-based exercise and education, and group messaging programs. However, while these interventions all demonstrated a positive effect on participant outcomes, the papers yielded some limitations; namely recruitment of populations that may not have completely represented the wider community of CVD sufferers. As a result, some papers had recruitment bias as it may have been possible that the participants were a subset of highly motivated individuals that were more inclined to pursue novel and social-focussed interventions. Hence, further research is required for the judicious implementation of social support interventions for older adults with CVD, with a focus on a wider range of individuals from all facets of society, to ensure an unbiased approach to improving patient outcomes.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This systematic review identified that face-to-face group-based interventions with exercise components may provide a basis for reducing loneliness and social isolation among older adults with CVD. Improvements were noted across social support, psychological wellbeing and quality of life. While improvements in physical measures were also noted in a small group of studies, these may not be attributed to enhanced social support, as interventions included a variety of lifestyle components, including exercise. Due to the limited number of high quality studies and heterogeneity of outcome measures, results do need to be interpreted with caution, highlighting the need for further research.
